content: Passengers or crew members who exhibit symptoms consistent with Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and have traveled to or stayed in a country reporting at least one confirmed case of EVD within 21 days prior to symptom onset may pose a risk to others if they have had direct contact with the affected individual, their bodily fluids, or heavily contaminated objects. The following measures should be implemented based on proximity to the index patient: 1. Passengers and crew with reported direct contact: Information about significant events during the flight should be obtained from the aircraft operator. Co-travelers and crew members who report direct body contact with the index case must undergo contact tracing. 2. Passengers seated adjacent to the index case: Since direct contact is the primary route of Ebola virus transmission, only passengers seated next to the index case (on the side, in front, behind, or across the aisle) should be included in contact tracing. 3. Staff cleaning the affected aircraft section: Cleaning staff working in the area where the sick passenger was seated or any other contaminated areas (e.g., toilets) must treat any remains of blood or body fluids as infectious. This includes cleaning heavily soiled surfaces (e.g., vomit or blood) and disposing of contaminated materials. Hand hygiene should be performed after removing personal protective equipment (PPE), either by using an alcohol-based hand rub for 20–30 seconds or washing hands with soap and water for 40–60 seconds if visibly dirty. Contaminated surfaces or objects should be cleaned and disinfected promptly using approved detergents or disinfectants. If the seat is made of non-cleanable fabric and is soiled with body fluids, it should be removed before the aircraft is used again. If the case is suspected or diagnosed after the passenger has left the aircraft, cleaning staff who worked in the affected area without wearing appropriate PPE should also undergo contact tracing. 4. Assessment of at-risk individuals: Passengers, crew members, and cleaning staff identified through contact tracing should be assessed for their specific level of exposure. For those at higher risk, regular temperature monitoring (twice daily) should continue for 21 days. 5. Post-arrival measures: If an individual who experienced symptoms during the flight is suspected of having EVD, similar measures should be applied after arrival. All at-risk individuals should be provided with information on how and where to seek medical care if they develop symptoms or require treatment. 6. Guidance for ships and shipping companies: Shipping companies must immediately notify the port health authority if a person on board is suspected of having EVD. The ship’s master, doctor, or designated health officer must be fully informed about EVD risks and trained in protective measures to prevent transmission. If a crew member or passenger presents with EVD-compatible symptoms (e.g., fever, weakness, muscle pain, headache, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding), the following precautions should be taken: Keep the affected person’s cabin doors closed unless they are placed in an isolation room. Provide information about EVD transmission risks to those caring for the patient or entering their cabin. Maintain a log of all individuals entering the cabin or isolation room, who should be considered contacts unless diagnostic tests are negative. Ensure that anyone entering the cabin or isolation room to care for the patient or clean the area uses PPE, including non-sterile gloves, a disposable impermeable long-sleeved gown, a medical mask, and eye protection (visor, goggles, or face shield). If impermeable gowns are unavailable, a waterproof apron should be worn over a non-impermeable gown. Rubber boots or closed, punctureand fluid-resistant shoes with overshoes should also be used. 7. Hand hygiene: Anyone providing care to the isolated individual must perform hand hygiene before and after contact with the patient, their belongings, or potentially contaminated objects/surfaces, and after removing PPE. This can be done using an alcohol-based hand rub for 20–30 seconds or washing hands with soap and water for 40–60 seconds if visibly dirty. 8. Movement and transport of the affected person: Limit the movement and transport of the affected individual to essential purposes only. If transport is necessary, the patient should wear a medical mask. 9. Cleaning and disinfection: Spills should be cleaned without spraying or using aerosols. Used linen, cloths, eating utensils, laundry, and other items in contact with the patient’s body fluids should be collected separately and disinfected to avoid contamination of the environment or contact with others. Disinfectants such as 0.5% chlorine solution or a solution containing 1000 ppm available free chlorine with a contact time of 30 minutes should be used. Cleaning should precede disinfection to prevent inactivation of disinfectants by organic matter. Soiled linen and cloths should not be reused and must be disposed of in infectious waste bags. 10. Waste management: All waste produced in the cabin or isolation room should be handled according to the ship’s protocol for clinical infectious waste. If an onboard incinerator is available, waste should be incinerated. If waste must be delivered ashore, special precautions are required, and the port authority should be informed before delivery. 11. Contact tracing: Begin contact tracing immediately. PPE is not necessary when interviewing asymptomatic individuals if a distance of one meter is maintained. Regular temperature monitoring (twice daily) for 21 days is recommended for those at risk. 12. Medical evacuation and reporting: In the event of a suspected EVD diagnosis on a ship, expert medical opinion should be sought immediately, and the event should be reported to the next port of call by the ship’s master. The affected individual should disembark in a manner that avoids contact with others and wear a medical mask. Personnel involved in medical evacuation should wear appropriate PPE, including a medical mask, long-sleeved gown, and eye protection. 13. Port authority coordination: Depending on the situation, the competent authority at the relevant port may need to arrange medical evacuation or special disembarkation and hospitalization procedures for the patient, as well as laboratory diagnosis. Shipping companies must facilitate obtaining information on the itinerary and contact details of individuals on board if exposure to infection is suspected. Countries may require arriving ships to complete and deliver the Maritime Declaration of Health (IHR Annex 8). Measures taken on board should also be documented on the IHR Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (IHR Annex 3).
